title: Across the echo bridge
note: ISBAR helps you identify yourself and the patient, explain the situation, give relevant background and assessment, and make a clear recommendation. Confirm the receiver’s response, responsibilities and review plan. Use accurate observations and the patient’s own concerns. Follow local escalation processes; never delay urgent help to finish a script.

start.speaker: Mira Vale · bridge courier
start.text: A brass messenger bird waits on Mira’s blanket. “I carry words across kingdoms,” she says, “but I can’t seem to make anyone hear mine. I feel dizzy when I sit up. I’m worried I’ll fall.” Rowan asks you to prepare a call to the ward clinician, who is across the echo bridge.

choices.label: Listen to Mira and help her stay safely seated
Ask her to walk to the bridge so the clinician can see her

walking.speaker: Sage Rowan
walking.text: Mira has told us she feels dizzy. Don’t ask her to walk unsupported to prove it. Stay with her, make the immediate situation safe and arrange assessment and help.

choices.label: Stay with Mira and listen

listen.speaker: Mira Vale
listen.text: “It started this afternoon. I nearly toppled when I tried to reach my bag. The bag isn’t important. The little bird is—it belonged to my sister.” You place her call bell within reach and explain that you will seek a review. Rowan stays beside her while you prepare the call.

choices.label: Check her identity and gather the current assessment
Tell her it is probably nothing before assessing

reassure.speaker: Your reflection
reassure.text: Reassurance should not dismiss a new symptom or concern. You can be calm without making a promise: “I’m listening. We’ll check what’s happening and get help.”

choices.label: Acknowledge the concern and gather the facts

prepare.speaker: Your bedside notes
prepare.text: Mira states her name and date of birth. You match these and the medical record number against her wristband and record. Your assessment finds that she is alert and speaking clearly, with dizziness on sitting. These fictional observations support this conversation exercise; they are not a universal escalation chart.

evidence.title: IDENTITY & CONTEXT
lines: Mira Vale · DOB 08 June 1994 · MRN LW-2013
Admitted yesterday with a wrist injury after a bridge fall
New dizziness this afternoon; almost fell reaching for her bag

evidence.title: CURRENT ASSESSMENT · 21:20
lines: Alert; speaking clearly; dizzy on sitting
Rowan is staying with her; clinician review needed

choices.label: Use the pocket card to organise an ISBAR call
Send only “the patient is unwell” through the bird

vague.speaker: The echo bridge
vague.text: The brass bird repeats your message exactly. Across the bridge comes the reply: “Which patient, where, and what has changed?” Magic can carry a message; it cannot supply missing information.

choices.label: Organise the call with ISBAR

identify.speaker: The receiving clinician · I / Identify
identify.text: The voice on the other end asks you to begin. Choose an opening that makes clear who is speaking, where you are and which patient needs review.

choices.label: “Wayfarer, RN in Lantern Ward, calling about Mira Vale, DOB 08 June 1994, MRN LW-2013.”
“It’s me, about the courier in the third bed.”

identify_retry.speaker: ISBAR pocket card
identify_retry.text: A role, location and patient identifiers help the receiver connect the message with the correct person. A bed number alone is not a patient identifier.

choices.label: Identify yourself, the ward and Mira using her identifiers

situation.speaker: The receiving clinician · S / Situation
situation.text: “Thank you. What is the immediate concern?” The bridge crackles with a distant storm. Keep your opening concern clear.

choices.label: “Mira has new dizziness when sitting and nearly fell. I’m concerned and requesting review.”
“The bird’s wings are squeaking and the ward has been quite busy.”

situation_retry.speaker: Sage Rowan
situation_retry.text: Start with the patient’s current problem and your concern. The receiver needs to know why this call matters before hearing the ward’s other stories.

choices.label: Explain the new dizziness and near-fall

background.speaker: The receiving clinician · B / Background
background.text: “What is the relevant background?” You glance at your notes rather than relying on the ward’s rumours.

choices.label: “Admitted yesterday after a bridge fall with a wrist injury; this dizziness is new this afternoon.”
“She must be dehydrated; I haven’t checked the history.”

background_retry.speaker: Your reflection
background_retry.text: Separate known facts from possible explanations. You can say what you are concerned about without presenting an unconfirmed cause as a diagnosis.

choices.label: Give the verified admission history and symptom onset

assessment.speaker: The receiving clinician · A / Assessment
assessment.text: “What have you found?” You have the current observations in front of you.

evidence.title: READ BACK YOUR FINDINGS
lines: 21:20 · alert and speaking clearly; dizziness on sitting
No cause has been established; worried about safe mobility

choices.label: Report the actual findings, time and concern about safe mobility
Say the observations are “normal” and leave out the dizziness

assessment_retry.speaker: ISBAR pocket card
assessment_retry.text: A summary like “normal” hides useful information. Share the actual findings and the patient’s symptom. A reassuring individual number does not erase a concern.

choices.label: Give the observations and describe the dizziness

recommendation.speaker: The receiving clinician · R / Recommendation
recommendation.text: “What do you need from me?” Mira watches the bird and waits for a plan she can understand.

choices.label: Request a prompt bedside review and agree what to monitor and when to escalate
“Just letting you know.” End the call without an agreed plan

recommendation_retry.speaker: Sage Rowan
recommendation_retry.text: A clear request helps turn information into action. Ask for the review Mira needs and confirm what should happen while you wait. If the response does not meet the concern, use the escalation pathway.

choices.label: Ask for a prompt review and an agreed interim plan

readback.speaker: The receiving clinician
readback.text: “I’ll come to Lantern Ward now. Please keep her supported, continue monitoring under the local plan and call again through the escalation pathway if there is any worsening.” Thunder swallows the final words. What do you do?

choices.label: Ask them to repeat the unclear part, then confirm the plan and responsibility
Guess what was said so the call can end quickly

readback_retry.speaker: The echo bridge
readback_retry.text: An uncertain message is a reason to clarify, not a test of confidence. You reconnect, ask for the missed words and read back the agreed actions.

choices.label: Confirm who is coming and the monitoring/escalation plan

patient_plan.speaker: Mira Vale
patient_plan.text: “So someone is coming? And Rowan will stay?” You explain the plan in plain language, confirm her understanding and document the call, response and agreed actions. A clinician arrives and takes over the review. The bird folds its wings.

choices.label: Ask Mira about the message she was carrying
Give Mira space to rest after explaining the plan

letter.speaker: Mira Vale
letter.text: “A letter to my sister. I wrote that I was fine. Couriers are meant to be brave.” She turns it over. “Perhaps I’ll write that I asked for help.” She offers you a tiny brass feather from the bird’s spare-parts pouch.

choices.label: Accept the feather as a reminder to make room for someone’s voice

rest_end.speaker: Mira Vale
rest_end.text: “Thank you for not making me tell the whole story twice.” She settles back while the clinician speaks with her. Rowan leaves a brass feather beside your pocket card: a small token for a message that reached the right person.

choices.label: Keep the feather with your ISBAR card

complete.speaker: The echo bridge
complete.text: A line of lights stretches across the bridge. You did not make the storm quieter. You made one person’s needs clear enough to cross it. Beyond the windows, the thunder is getting closer.
